text.p: In overnight commodity markets, zinc and aluminium prices surged on short-covering on the London Metal Exchange. Nickel again dropped heavily.
The gold price dropped another US$2 an ounce to US$318.50 as sentiment turned bearish again amid talk of new producer hedging.
Oil prices fell on renewed fears about new Iraqi supplies.
Wheat prices closed up in Chicago on strong U.S. exports.
The CRB index closed down 0.79 at 242.81

On the London Metal Exchange overnight, Zinc and aluminium surged on Tuesday afternoon as short-covering and speculative buying tickled the upside, while nickel headed in the other direction, piling up more losses.
Three months aluminium ended the afternoon kerb $20.50 firmer at $1,741.50 per tonne after touching a high of $1,743.

Traders said some players went short in the morning as prices headed down, touching a low of $1,712. But it held at the lows and investment house buying during lunch sent the market into the plus column.

The cash/threes backwardation flared to $5/$10 from $3/$7 on Tuesday. Three months zinc marched up to the highest levels since prices crashed last week, hitting a high of $1,538 after earlier hitting a low of $1,505. But selling took the froth off the highs and prices ended the kerb $30 firmer at $1,528.
The market is still trying to puzzle out China's position after reports of huge short positions held by Chinese smelters.
Nickel lost more ground, failing to defend the $7,180 support level and falling $100 to a low of $7,160, where it closed. Next support was pegged at $7,100 and $7,010.
Copper edged higher, but was capped again by stubborn resistance at $2,300, ending $13 firmer at $2,298.
The cash/threes narrowed again by a couple of dollars to a $22/$27 backwardation.
COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mostly lower Wednesday, with the exception of silver, but volumes were significantly lower than Tuesday.

"Tomorrow could be an interesting day in gold, and I would think there is still some serious downside risk as basically there's just been one major player supporting the market," Swiss Bank New York precious metals dealer, Greg Drury, said.

"About 50 percent of world gold production is probably uneconomic at current prices, and the longer gold stays down at these levels, the sooner some miners are going to have to do some more hedging," he said.

"About 50 percent of Australian reserves are currently hedged, but only about 12 percent of North American reserves and 10 percent of South African reserves are hedged, so either one major producing country is very overhedged or two countries are underhedged."
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $318.30/80, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $319.35 and the New York close Tuesday at $320.20/70.
CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed higher on prospects for increased exports of U.S. wheat, traders said.

European traders said Iraq bought 50,000 tonnes of U.S. hard red winter wheat. U.S. wheat prices returned to competitive levels after a break earlier this week and the EU late last week imposed a tax on wheat exports which was underpinning wheat futures. Wheat closed 2-1/2 to 10 cents per bushel higher, with September up 8-3/4 at $3.62 a bushel.

Oil traders on Wednesday were bracing for a renewed wave of Iraqi oil exports which analysts said would spell the end of a rally on world crude markets. Prices would probably prove resilient in the short term but they warned of a looming imbalance on oil markets in the months ahead. London September North Sea Brent blend futures closed 34 cents lower at $19.18 a barrel. Brent has recovered from its low for the year at $17.30 in early June.
